history.q: Which royal warship sank in Stockholm harbour on its maiden voyage in 1628?
history.fact: Raised from the seabed in 1961, the Vasa is the world's best-preserved 17th-century ship and now fills its own museum in Stockholm.

history.q: Which Swedish king, the "Lion of the North", was killed at the Battle of Lützen in 1632?
history.fact: Gustavus Adolphus's intervention in the Thirty Years' War turned Sweden into one of Europe's great powers.

history.q: Which Scandinavian seafarers raided and traded far from Sweden between roughly 800 and 1050 CE?
history.fact: Swedish Vikings travelled east along Russian rivers to Constantinople, where some served in the Byzantine emperor's Varangian Guard.

history.q: Which king, elected in 1523, is regarded as the founder of the modern Swedish state?
history.fact: Sweden's National Day, 6 June, marks Gustav Vasa's election as king after he led the break from the Kalmar Union.

history.q: What official stance did Sweden take during the Second World War?
history.fact: Sweden has not fought a war since a short campaign against Norway in 1814, one of the longest runs of peace of any nation.

history.q: Which union, formed in 1397, joined Sweden with Denmark and Norway under a single monarch?
history.fact: It is named after the Swedish town of Kalmar, where Eric of Pomerania was crowned king of all three realms.

history.q: To which empire did Sweden lose Finland in 1809?
history.fact: Finland had been part of the Swedish realm for around 600 years before it became a grand duchy of the Russian Empire.

history.q: Which country peacefully dissolved its union with Sweden in 1905?
history.fact: In a referendum that August, Norwegians backed independence by 368,208 votes to just 184.

history.q: Which Swedish diplomat saved thousands of Jews in Budapest in 1944 by issuing protective passports?
history.fact: Wallenberg vanished into Soviet custody in 1945; Swedish authorities formally declared him dead in 2016.

history.q: Which Swedish queen abdicated in 1654 and later converted to Catholicism?
history.fact: Christina settled in Rome and is one of only a handful of women buried in St Peter's Basilica.

history.q: Which French marshal was elected Swedish crown prince in 1810, founding the present royal dynasty?
history.fact: He became King Charles XIV John in 1818, and every Swedish monarch since has descended from him.

history.q: Which Swedish king was defeated by Peter the Great at the Battle of Poltava in 1709?
history.fact: After Poltava, Charles XII fled south and spent about five years as a guest of the Ottoman Empire.

history.q: Which Swedish king was fatally shot at a masked ball in Stockholm's Royal Opera in 1792?
history.fact: The assassination inspired Giuseppe Verdi's opera Un ballo in maschera (A Masked Ball).

history.q: Which 1658 treaty transferred the province of Skåne from Denmark to Sweden?
history.fact: Charles X Gustav forced the deal after marching his army across the frozen Danish straits in the depths of winter.

history.q: Which Swedish count organised the "White Buses" that rescued concentration camp prisoners in 1945?
history.fact: Bernadotte later became the UN's mediator in Palestine and was assassinated in Jerusalem in 1948.

history.q: Which walled town on the island of Gotland was a leading member of the medieval Hanseatic League?
history.fact: Visby's medieval ring wall, about 3.4 km long, is one of the best preserved in Scandinavia and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: Swedish engineer Salomon August Andrée set off by hydrogen balloon in 1897 to reach where?
history.fact: The crew's fate was a mystery until their last camp was found in 1930, along with film that could still be developed.

history.q: Which Swedish king was deposed by army officers in 1809 after the loss of Finland?
history.fact: Gustav IV Adolf spent the rest of his life in exile and died in Switzerland in 1837.

history.q: The Swedish victory at the Battle of Breitenfeld in 1631 was fought during which war?
history.fact: Gustavus Adolphus's defeat of the Imperial general Tilly at Breitenfeld was the first great Protestant victory of the war.

history.q: Which 1721 treaty ended the Great Northern War and Sweden's era as a great power?
history.fact: Sweden ceded Livonia, Estonia, Ingria and part of Karelia to Peter the Great's Russia.

history.q: What name is given to the period from 1719 to 1772 when Sweden's parliament dominated its kings?
history.fact: Rival parliamentary factions, nicknamed the Hats and the Caps, ran the country until Gustav III's coup in 1772.

history.q: Which Danish king ordered the 1520 executions known as the Stockholm Bloodbath?
history.fact: The killings turned Swedes against the Kalmar Union, and the king is still remembered in Sweden as "Christian the Tyrant".

history.q: Which runestone in Östergötland bears the longest known runic inscription?
history.fact: Carved in the 800s, its more than 700 runes include riddles and allusions that scholars still debate.

history.q: At which 1700 battle did 18-year-old Charles XII defeat a much larger Russian army in a snowstorm?
history.fact: The victory at Narva, in present-day Estonia, made Charles XII famous across Europe at the start of the Great Northern War.

history.q: Which Swedish west-coast city was founded by Gustavus Adolphus in 1621?
history.fact: Dutch engineers helped lay out its canals, and the city gave Sweden a port on the North Sea beyond Denmark's control of the Sound.

technology.q: Which Swedish chemist invented dynamite?
technology.fact: Nobel patented dynamite in 1867 and left most of his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes, first awarded in 1901.

technology.q: Which Swedish astronomer devised a 100-degree temperature scale in 1742?
technology.fact: Celsius originally set 0 as the boiling point of water and 100 as freezing; the scale was flipped after his death.

technology.q: Which Swedish botanist created the two-part Latin naming system used for species, such as Homo sapiens?
technology.fact: Linnaeus's Species Plantarum of 1753 is the official starting point for the scientific names of plants.

technology.q: Which flat-pack furniture company did Ingvar Kamprad found in 1943?
technology.fact: The name combines his initials with Elmtaryd, his family's farm, and Agunnaryd, his home village in Småland.

technology.q: Which Swedish carmaker introduced the modern three-point seat belt in 1959?
technology.fact: Engineer Nils Bohlin designed it, and Volvo let other manufacturers use the patented design for free.

technology.q: Which music-streaming service was founded in Stockholm in 2006?
technology.fact: Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon founded Spotify, which launched its service in 2008.

technology.q: Lars Magnus Ericsson's Stockholm workshop, opened in 1876, grew into a giant in which industry?
technology.fact: Ericsson began by repairing telegraph equipment and became one of the world's leading makers of mobile network gear.

technology.q: Which internet calling service did Swede Niklas Zennström co-found in 2003?
technology.fact: Skype was co-founded with Dane Janus Friis and built by Estonian programmers; Microsoft bought it in 2011.

technology.q: Which Stockholm game studio created the best-selling video game Minecraft?
technology.fact: Minecraft was created by Markus "Notch" Persson, and Microsoft bought Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion.

technology.q: Which Swedish chemist discovered oxygen independently in the early 1770s?
technology.fact: Scheele also first produced chlorine and identified several organic acids, all while working as a pharmacist.

technology.q: Which Swedish chemist introduced the letter-based chemical symbols, such as H and O, still used today?
technology.fact: Berzelius also helped discover the elements cerium, selenium and thorium.

technology.q: Which Swedish scientist calculated in 1896 that more carbon dioxide in the air would warm the Earth?
technology.fact: Arrhenius won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his theory of how salts split into ions in solution.

technology.q: Which carton-packaging company was founded by Ruben Rausing in Lund?
technology.fact: Its first tetrahedron-shaped cartons, used for cream, appeared in 1952.

technology.q: Which Swedish inventor is credited with the modern adjustable spanner (wrench)?
technology.fact: Johansson ran a workshop in Enköping, and his tools were sold worldwide through the firm that became Bahco.

technology.q: Which Swedish-born engineer designed the ironclad USS Monitor for the Union Navy?
technology.fact: Ericsson also pioneered the screw propeller; his body was returned to Sweden in 1890 aboard the cruiser USS Baltimore.

technology.q: Which Swedish inventor built a centrifugal cream separator in the 1870s?
technology.fact: His company became Alfa Laval, and he also built pioneering high-speed steam turbines.

technology.q: At which Swedish company was Bluetooth wireless technology first developed?
technology.fact: It is named after the Danish Viking king Harald Bluetooth, and its logo merges his runic initials.

technology.q: Which tiny unit of length, one ten-billionth of a metre, is named after a Swedish physicist?
technology.fact: Anders Jonas Ångström was a founder of spectroscopy and showed that the Sun's spectrum contains hydrogen.

technology.q: In 1958, the first fully implanted cardiac pacemaker was fitted at which Swedish hospital?
technology.fact: The patient, Arne Larsson, received 26 pacemakers over his lifetime and outlived both of the device's inventors.

technology.q: Which Swedish engineer won the 1912 Nobel Prize in Physics for an automatic valve used in lighthouses?
technology.fact: Dalén was blinded in an explosion the same year, yet went on to invent the AGA cooker.

technology.q: Which company commercialised the absorption refrigerator invented by Swedish students Baltzar von Platen and Carl Munters?
technology.fact: Their design has no moving parts, which is why it is still used in silent hotel minibars and caravan fridges.

technology.q: Swedish machinist Carl Edvard Johansson invented which precision measuring tools?
technology.fact: Henry Ford was so impressed that he hired Johansson, and the blocks are still nicknamed "Jo blocks".

technology.q: Which Swedish physicist won the 1970 Nobel Prize for his work on magnetohydrodynamics and plasmas?
technology.fact: Alfvén waves, which ripple through plasmas such as the Sun's atmosphere, are named after him.

technology.q: The elements yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium are all named after which Swedish village?
technology.fact: A single quarry at Ytterby, in the Stockholm archipelago, yielded minerals that led to the discovery of several new elements.

technology.q: Which Swedish electrical company, founded in 1883, later merged with Brown Boveri to form ABB?
technology.fact: ASEA and Switzerland's Brown, Boveri & Cie combined in 1988 to create one of the world's largest engineering groups.

art.q: Which Swedish pop group won the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest with "Waterloo"?
art.fact: The band's name is an acronym of its members' first names: Agnetha, Björn, Benny and Anni-Frid.

art.q: Which Swedish author created Pippi Longstocking?
art.fact: Lindgren's books have been translated into more than 100 languages.

art.q: Which Swedish director made the 1957 film The Seventh Seal, in which a knight plays chess with Death?
art.fact: The image of the knight and the hooded figure of Death on a beach is one of the most parodied scenes in cinema.

art.q: Which Swedish journalist wrote The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo?
art.fact: Larsson died in 2004, before any of his Millennium novels were published.

art.q: Which Swedish actress starred opposite Humphrey Bogart in Casablanca?
art.fact: Ingrid Bergman won three Academy Awards during her career.

art.q: Which Swedish-born Hollywood star famously said "I want to be alone" in the 1932 film Grand Hotel?
art.fact: Garbo retired from film in 1941 and spent the rest of her life avoiding publicity in New York.

art.q: Which Swedish DJ and producer released the hits "Levels" and "Wake Me Up"?
art.fact: Stockholm's giant globe-shaped arena, the Globen, was renamed Avicii Arena in his honour in 2021.

art.q: Which Swedish duo recorded "It Must Have Been Love" and "The Look"?
art.fact: "It Must Have Been Love" became a worldwide hit in 1990 on the soundtrack of the film Pretty Woman.

art.q: Which Swedish rock band had a 1986 hit with "The Final Countdown"?
art.fact: The song reached number one in the UK and many other countries, and its synth riff still blares in sports arenas.

art.q: Which Swedish writer became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1909?
art.fact: Her Wonderful Adventures of Nils, about a boy flying over Sweden on a goose, was written as a geography reader for schools.

art.q: Which Swedish playwright wrote Miss Julie (1888)?
art.fact: Strindberg was also an expressive painter whose stormy seascapes now hang in major museums.

art.q: Which Swedish painter is famous for watercolours of family life at his home in Sundborn?
art.fact: His book of paintings Ett hem (A Home) helped shape the bright, airy style of Swedish interiors.

art.q: Which Swedish artist painted abstract works from 1906, years before Kandinsky?
art.fact: She asked that her abstract paintings stay hidden for 20 years after her death; a 2018 Guggenheim show drew record crowds.

art.q: Which painter from Mora in Dalarna was celebrated for his portraits, nudes and etchings?
art.fact: Zorn's portrait sitters included US Presidents Grover Cleveland and William Howard Taft.

art.q: In which Stockholm building is the Nobel Prize banquet held?
art.fact: Architect Ragnar Östberg planned to plaster the Blue Hall, but liked the bare brick so much that he left it unpainted.

art.q: Which Swedish author wrote The Emigrants novels about Småland farmers moving to Minnesota?
art.fact: Jan Troell filmed the story in 1971 with Max von Sydow and Liv Ullmann in the lead roles.

art.q: Which musical did ABBA's Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus write with lyricist Tim Rice?
art.fact: Its single "One Night in Bangkok" became an international hit in 1984.

art.q: Which Swedish author created the detective Kurt Wallander?
art.fact: Wallander works in the southern town of Ystad, which now draws fans on Wallander-themed walking tours.

art.q: Which Stockholm cemetery, designed by Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
art.fact: The Woodland Cemetery blends graves into a pine forest, and Greta Garbo is buried there.

art.q: Which Swedish poet won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: A 1990 stroke left him barely able to speak, but he kept writing and playing the piano with his left hand.

art.q: Which 18th-century Swedish poet and songwriter wrote Fredman's Epistles?
art.fact: Bellman's songs about Stockholm's taverns, drinkers and dreamers are still sung by Swedes today.

art.q: Which Ingmar Bergman film won four Academy Awards, including Best Foreign Language Film, in 1984?
art.fact: Bergman also made a five-hour television version of the story, set in a wealthy family in Uppsala.

art.q: Which Swedish sculptor's former home on Lidingö is now an open-air museum of his work?
art.fact: Milles taught for two decades at Cranbrook Academy in Michigan, and many of his fountains stand in the United States.

art.q: Which Swedish director won the Palme d'Or in 2017 for The Square?
art.fact: The satire follows the chief curator of a Stockholm art museum whose life unravels around an art installation.

art.q: Which architect designed Drottningholm Palace, the Swedish royal family's home outside Stockholm?
art.fact: The palace's 1766 court theatre still works with its original wooden stage machinery.

politics.q: What is the name of Sweden's national parliament?
politics.fact: Its 349 members are elected for four-year terms by proportional representation.

politics.q: Which king acceded to the Swedish throne in 1973?
politics.fact: In 2018 he overtook the medieval king Magnus IV to become the longest-reigning monarch in Swedish history.

politics.q: Which royal became heir to the Swedish throne after a 1980 law gave the crown to the eldest child regardless of sex?
politics.fact: Sweden was the first monarchy to adopt equal succession, which moved her ahead of her younger brother Carl Philip.

politics.q: In which year did Sweden join the European Union?
politics.fact: Sweden joined at the same time as Austria and Finland, after a referendum in November 1994.

politics.q: Which currency did Swedish voters reject in a 2003 referendum?
politics.fact: About 56% voted no, so Sweden kept the krona even though it is an EU member.

politics.q: What type of state is Sweden?
politics.fact: Under the 1974 Instrument of Government, the monarch's duties are purely ceremonial and representative.

politics.q: Which Swedish prime minister was shot dead on a Stockholm street in 1986?
politics.fact: Palme was walking home from a cinema with his wife, without bodyguards, when he was shot on Sveavägen.

politics.q: Unlike the other Nobel Prizes presented in Stockholm, the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in which city?
politics.fact: Nobel's will gave the Peace Prize to a committee of Norway's parliament; Norway and Sweden were then in union.

politics.q: Which Swedish teenager began a school strike for the climate outside the Riksdag in August 2018?
politics.fact: Her hand-painted sign, "Skolstrejk för klimatet", launched the worldwide Fridays for Future movement.

politics.q: Which Swede served as UN Secretary-General from 1953 until his death in 1961?
politics.fact: Killed in a plane crash in Northern Rhodesia, he remains the only person awarded the Nobel Peace Prize posthumously.

politics.q: Which public office, created in Sweden in 1809, has given its Swedish name to similar posts worldwide?
politics.fact: The parliamentary ombudsman was set up to make sure that officials and courts obey the law.

politics.q: Sweden's Freedom of the Press Act of 1766 is famous for being what?
choices: The world's first law protecting press freedom
The first law requiring state censors
politics.fact: The same act introduced the right of public access to official documents, still a cornerstone of Swedish government.

politics.q: Which party held power in Sweden for 44 years from 1932, apart from a brief break in 1936?
politics.fact: Social Democrat Tage Erlander led the government for 23 unbroken years, from 1946 to 1969.

politics.q: Which Swedish word describes the vision of society as a caring "people's home"?
politics.fact: Social Democrat leader Per Albin Hansson popularised the idea in a famous 1928 speech.

politics.q: Who was Sweden's prime minister throughout the Second World War?
politics.fact: Hansson died suddenly in 1946 after a heart attack at a Stockholm tram stop.

politics.q: Which Swedish Social Democrat shared the 1921 Nobel Peace Prize?
politics.fact: In 1920 Branting became Sweden's first Social Democratic prime minister.

politics.q: In which year did Swedish women first vote in a general election?
politics.fact: Five women won seats in the Riksdag in that first election.

politics.q: In which decade did Sweden's two-chamber Riksdag become a single chamber?
politics.fact: The bicameral parliament created in 1866 was replaced by a unicameral Riksdag in 1971.

politics.q: The Swedish Riksdag traces its origins to a 1435 meeting in which town?
politics.fact: For centuries the Riksdag of the Estates had four chambers: nobility, clergy, burghers and peasants.

politics.q: Which Swedish prime minister of 1991-1994 later served as foreign minister from 2006 to 2014?
politics.fact: Bildt also served as an EU and UN peace envoy in the former Yugoslavia during the 1990s.

politics.q: Which prime minister led Sweden's centre-right "Alliance" government from 2006 to 2014?
politics.fact: The Alliance brought together the Moderates, Centre Party, Liberals and Christian Democrats.

politics.q: Under Sweden's 1974 Instrument of Government, who proposes a new prime minister to the Riksdag?
politics.fact: Before the reform this was a task of the monarch; now the Speaker holds talks with party leaders first.

politics.q: What is the name of the Swedish prime minister's official residence in Stockholm?
politics.fact: The townhouse has been the official residence since 1995; nearby Rosenbad holds the Government Offices.

politics.q: What share of the national vote must a party win to gain seats in the Riksdag?
politics.fact: A party can also qualify by winning 12% of the vote in a single constituency.

politics.q: Who was Sweden's prime minister from 1996 to 2006?
politics.fact: Persson chaired the EU when Sweden held its first presidency of the Council, in 2001.

current-affairs.q: In March 2024, Sweden became the 32nd member of which alliance?
current-affairs.fact: Sweden applied together with Finland in May 2022, ending more than 200 years of military non-alignment.

current-affairs.q: Who became Sweden's first female prime minister in November 2021?
current-affairs.fact: She resigned hours after her first election when her budget failed, then was voted in again five days later.

current-affairs.q: Which Moderate Party leader became Sweden's prime minister in October 2022?
current-affairs.fact: He formed a coalition with the Christian Democrats and Liberals, backed in parliament by the Sweden Democrats.

current-affairs.q: Which Swedish city hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in May 2024?
current-affairs.fact: It was Malmö's third time as host, after 1992 and 2013.

current-affairs.q: Which Swedish singer won Eurovision 2023 with the song "Tattoo"?
current-affairs.fact: Having also won with "Euphoria" in 2012, she became the first woman to win the contest twice.

current-affairs.q: In 2019, which Swedish climate activist crossed the Atlantic by sailing yacht to attend a UN summit in New York?
current-affairs.fact: She sailed on the racing yacht Malizia II to avoid flying, and Time named her Person of the Year that December.

current-affairs.q: At the Paris Olympics in August 2024, Swede Armand "Mondo" Duplantis set a world record in which event?
current-affairs.fact: He cleared 6.25 m in Paris to defend the Olympic title he first won in Tokyo.

current-affairs.q: In spring 2020, Sweden drew global attention for avoiding which COVID-19 measure used across most of Europe?
current-affairs.fact: Sweden relied largely on voluntary recommendations and kept schools for younger children open.

current-affairs.q: Which Swedish striker announced his retirement while playing for AC Milan in June 2023?
current-affairs.fact: He retired as Sweden's all-time top international scorer, with 62 goals.

current-affairs.q: Which Swedish battery maker, once hailed as Europe's answer to Asian rivals, filed for bankruptcy in March 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Founded by former Tesla executives, it had built a giant battery factory near Skellefteå in northern Sweden.

current-affairs.q: In January 2023, Sweden took over which rotating six-month presidency?
choices: The Council of the European Union
current-affairs.fact: It was Sweden's third EU Council presidency, after 2001 and 2009.

current-affairs.q: Which country's parliament was the last to approve Sweden's NATO membership, in February 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Turkey's parliament had approved Sweden's bid a month earlier, in January 2024.

current-affairs.q: Swedish geneticist Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on what?
choices: The genomes of extinct human relatives
current-affairs.fact: His father, Sune Bergström, won the same prize in 1982.

current-affairs.q: Which party finished second in Sweden's September 2022 general election?
current-affairs.fact: The Social Democrats remained the largest party, with about 30% of the vote.

current-affairs.q: In August 2025, Kiruna's landmark wooden church was moved about 5 km to make way for what?
current-affairs.fact: The 1912 church, voted one of Sweden's most beautiful buildings, travelled on giant trailers at walking pace.

current-affairs.q: In January 2024, Marcus Wandt became the second Swede in space, flying to where?
current-affairs.fact: The first Swede in space was Christer Fuglesang, who flew on the Space Shuttle in 2006.

current-affairs.q: In January 2023, a new launch complex for orbital satellites was inaugurated at Esrange, near which Swedish city?
current-affairs.fact: Esrange has launched research rockets and high-altitude balloons from Swedish Lapland since 1966.

current-affairs.q: Where did Sweden finish at the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup?
current-affairs.fact: Beating co-hosts Australia 2-0 gave Sweden its fourth third-place finish at a Women's World Cup.

current-affairs.q: In June 2021, which Swedish prime minister became the first to lose a parliamentary vote of no confidence?
current-affairs.fact: Löfven resigned but was voted back into office by the Riksdag a few weeks later.

current-affairs.q: In June 2020, Swedish prosecutors named which man as Olof Palme's likely killer and closed the case?
current-affairs.fact: Engström, nicknamed the "Skandia Man" after his workplace, had died in 2000, so no charges could be brought.

current-affairs.q: Which Ruben Östlund film won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in May 2022?
current-affairs.fact: It made Östlund one of only a handful of directors to win the Palme d'Or twice.

current-affairs.q: Who was re-elected Speaker of the Riksdag after Sweden's September 2022 election?
current-affairs.fact: As Speaker, the Moderate politician also led the talks that produced Sweden's next prime minister.

current-affairs.q: In September 2022, explosions damaged which Baltic gas pipelines, partly inside Sweden's economic zone?
current-affairs.fact: Sweden closed its own investigation in February 2024, saying the case did not fall under Swedish jurisdiction.

current-affairs.q: In 2019, the glacier-capped south summit of which mountain lost its status as Sweden's highest point?
current-affairs.fact: As its ice cap melted, the rocky north summit, at about 2,097 m, became the highest point in Sweden.

current-affairs.q: Which Swedish golfer finished runner-up at his first Masters Tournament in April 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Åberg finished second to Scottie Scheffler at Augusta, in his first major championship.

general.q: What is the capital of Sweden?
general.fact: Stockholm is spread over 14 islands where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic Sea.

general.q: What is Sweden's currency?
general.fact: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, founded in 1668, is the oldest central bank still operating.

general.q: What are the colours of the Swedish flag?
general.fact: Like its Nordic neighbours' flags, it has a cross set off-centre towards the flagpole.

general.q: Around what do Swedes traditionally dance at Midsummer?
general.fact: A favourite Midsummer dance is "Små grodorna", in which dancers hop around the pole like little frogs.

general.q: Which Swedish classic is traditionally served with lingonberry jam, gravy and potatoes?
general.fact: IKEA's restaurants and food shops reportedly sell around a billion meatballs a year.

general.q: What is "fika" in Swedish culture?
choices: A coffee break with something sweet
general.fact: Many workplaces build fika into the day, often with a cinnamon bun, or kanelbulle.

general.q: Which Swedish tennis player won five Wimbledon singles titles in a row from 1976 to 1980?
general.fact: Borg also won the French Open six times, and retired from top-level tennis aged just 26.

general.q: Which Indigenous people, traditionally reindeer herders, live in northern Sweden?
general.fact: Sápmi, the Sámi homeland, stretches across Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula.

general.q: On 13 December, Swedes hold candlelit processions in honour of which saint?
general.fact: The Lucia leader wears a crown of candles, and saffron buns called lussekatter are eaten.

general.q: Which is Sweden's largest lake, and also the largest in the European Union?
general.fact: Vänern covers about 5,650 square kilometres.

general.q: What is the Swedish right that lets everyone roam, picnic and camp in most of the countryside?
general.fact: The "everyman's right" comes with a duty: do not disturb and do not destroy.

general.q: Which Swedish word means "just the right amount"?
general.fact: Lagom is often called the key to the Swedish approach to life: not too much, not too little.

general.q: In which Swedish city is a giant straw Christmas goat famously, and often, set on fire?
general.fact: First put up in 1966, the Gävle Goat has been burned in many years despite guards and fireproofing.

general.q: Which is Sweden's largest island?
general.fact: Gotland is famous for its limestone sea stacks, called raukar, and more than 90 medieval churches.

general.q: Which bridge links Malmö with Copenhagen?
general.fact: Opened in 2000, the crossing dives into a 4 km tunnel via an artificial island before reaching Denmark.

general.q: Which pungent Swedish delicacy is made from fermented Baltic herring?
general.fact: The cans often bulge from continued fermentation, so they are usually opened outdoors.

general.q: Which ski race, held each March, runs 90 km from Sälen to Mora?
general.fact: First held in 1922, it commemorates Gustav Vasa's legendary flight on skis in the 1520s.

general.q: Which is Sweden's second-largest city?
general.fact: Gothenburg is Volvo's home city and has Liseberg, one of Scandinavia's largest amusement parks.

general.q: In which Lapland village was the original Icehotel built?
general.fact: Since 1989 it has been rebuilt each winter from blocks of ice cut from the nearby Torne River.

general.q: Which long-distance hiking trail runs about 440 km through Lapland from Abisko to Hemavan?
general.fact: Its name means "the King's Trail", and it passes close to Kebnekaise, Sweden's highest mountain.

general.q: Which Swedish waterway, opened in 1832, was dug largely by some 58,000 soldiers?
general.fact: Construction took 22 years, creating a route from Lake Vänern across Sweden toward the Baltic.

general.q: Which roadless national park in Lapland is often called one of Europe's last great wildernesses?
general.fact: Sarek has almost no marked trails, huts or bridges, and is part of the Laponia World Heritage Site.

general.q: Which Stockholm open-air museum, founded in 1891, displays historic buildings moved from across Sweden?
general.fact: Founded by Artur Hazelius, Skansen is often called the world's first open-air museum.

general.q: In which province is the "Kingdom of Crystal", home to glassworks such as Kosta and Orrefors?
general.fact: The Kosta glassworks dates back to 1742.

general.q: The village of Nusnäs, near Mora, is famous for making which Swedish souvenir?
general.fact: Most are painted bright red with a floral harness in the traditional kurbits style.
